source_text: Sed nobis dii sunt, inquitis. Et quomodo vos e contrario impii et sacrilegi et irreligiosi erga deos vestros deprehendimini, qui quos praesumitis esse, negligatis, quos timetis, destruatis, quos etiam vindicatis, illudatis? Recognoscite, si mentiar. Primo quidem, cum alii alios colitis, utique quos non colitis offenditis. Praelatio alterius sine contumelia alterius non potest procedere, quia nec electio sine reprobatione. Jam ergo contemnitis quos reprobatis, quos reprobando offendere non timetis. Nam ut supra perstrinximus, status dei cujusque in senatus aestimatione pendebat. Deus non erat, quem homo consultus noluisset et nolendo damnasset. Domesticos deos, quos lares dicitis, domestica potestate tractatis pignerando, venditando, demutando aliquando in cacabulum de Saturno, aliquando in trullam de Minerva, ut quisque contritus atque contusus est, dum diu colitur, ut quisque dominus sanctiorem expertus est domesticam necessitatem. Publicos aeque publico jure foedatis, quos in hastario vectigales habetis. Sic Capitolium, sic olitorium forum petitur; sub eadem voce praeconis, sub eadem hasta, sub eadem annotatione quaestoris divinitas addicta conducitur. Sed enim agri tributo onusti viliores, hominum capita stipendio censa ignobiliora; nam hae sunt notae captivitatis. Dii vero qui magis tributarii, magis sancti; imo qui magis sancti, magis tributarii. Majestas quaestuaria efficitur. Circuit cauponas religio mendicans. Exigitis mercedem pro solo templi, pro aditu sacri; non licet deos nosse gratis, venales sunt. Quid omnino ad honorandos eos facitis, quod non etiam mortuis vestris conferatis? aedes proinde, aras proinde. Idem habitus et insignia in statuis. Ut aetas, ut ars, ut negotium mortui fuit, ita deus est. Quo differt ab epulo Jovis silicernium, a simpulo obba, ab haruspice pollinctor? nam et haruspex mortuis apparet. Sed digne imperatoribus defunctis honorem divinitatis dicatis, quibus et viventibus eum addicitis. Accepto ferent dii vestri, imo gratulabuntur, quod pares eis fiant domini sui. Sed quum Larentinam, publicum scortum, velim saltem Laidem aut Phrynen, inter Junones et Cereres ac Dianas adoratis; quum Simonem Magum statua et inscriptione sancti dei inauguratis; quum de paedagogiis aulicis nescio quem synodi deum facitis: licet non nobiliores dii veteres, tamen contumeliam a vobis deputabunt, hoc et aliis licuisse, quod solis antiquitas contulit.
pass_a_gloss: But you say that we have gods. And how, on the other hand, you are caught being impious and sacrilegious and irreligious towards your gods, who you presume to be, you neglect, whom you fear, you destroy, whom you also avenge, you mock? Recognize if I am lying. First, indeed, when you worship some and not others, certainly you offend those whom you do not worship. The preference for one without the contempt of another cannot occur, because neither can election occur without rejection. Now, therefore, you despise those whom you reject, whom, by rejecting, you do not fear to offend. For, as we have mentioned above, the status of each god was pending in the senate's estimation. A god was not one whom a consulted man would not have wanted and, by not wanting, would have condemned. The household gods, whom you call lares, you treat with domestic power by pawning, selling, and sometimes changing into a chamber pot of Saturn, sometimes into a ladle of Minerva, as each one is worn out and battered, while being worshipped for a long time, as each master has experienced domestic necessity. You equally defile the public ones with public law, whom you have as taxable in the auction. Thus, the Capitolium, thus the vegetable market is sought; under the same voice of the auctioneer, under the same spear, under the same annotation of the quaestor, the divinity is sold and leased. But indeed, the fields burdened with tribute are cheaper, the heads of men assessed with a tax are more ignoble; for these are the marks of captivity. But truly, the gods who are more tributary, are more holy; or rather, who are more holy, are more tributary. The majesty is made mercenary. The religion goes around the taverns begging. You demand a fee for the temple floor, for the entrance to the sacred place; it is not allowed to know the gods for free, they are for sale. What, in any case, do you do to honor them, which you also do not confer on your dead? The buildings, therefore, the altars, therefore. The same attire and insignia are on the statues. As the age, as the art, as the business of the dead person was, so is the god. In what way does the silicernium of Jupiter differ from the feast, the obba from the simpulum, the pollinctor from the haruspex? For even the haruspex appears to the dead. But it is fitting that you give the honor of divinity to the deceased emperors, to whom you also attribute it while they are living. Your gods will accept it, or rather, they will congratulate, because their masters are made equal to them. But when you worship Larentina, a public prostitute, or at least Lais or Phryne, among the Junos and Ceres and Dianas; when you consecrate Simon Magus with a statue and an inscription of a holy god; when you make some unknown synod god from the palace pedagogues: although the older gods may not be more noble, yet they will consider it an insult from you, that this has been allowed to others, which only antiquity has conferred on them.

pass_b_english: You claim you have gods too. Fine — then explain how you get caught being impious, sacrilegious, and irreligious toward your own deities. You presume they exist, yet you neglect them. You fear them, yet you destroy them. You claim to avenge them, yet you mock them. Check the record if you think I'm lying.

Start with the obvious: when you worship some gods and ignore others, you inevitably offend the ones you snub. You can't elevate one without contempt for the other, because there is no election without rejection. So you despise the gods you reject, and you don't even fear offending them by that rejection.

As we noted earlier, every god's standing hung on the senate's vote. A deity wasn't a god unless a consulted senator wanted him; by refusing to want him, the senate condemned him. You treat your household gods — your Lares — like household property: you pawn them, sell them, melt them down into a chamber pot for Saturn or a ladle for Minerva, whichever one's worn out and battered after years of worship, whichever one's master has felt the pinch of domestic necessity.

You defile the public gods just as badly under public law. You put them up for auction as taxable assets. The Capitolium, the vegetable market — it's all the same: same auctioneer's voice, same spear, same quaestor's notation. Divinity is sold and leased like any other lot. Fields burdened with tribute go cheaper; human heads counted for the poll tax are more ignoble — those are the marks of captivity. But the gods? The more tribute they owe, the holier they are; or rather, the holier they are, the more tribute they owe. Majesty has become a revenue stream. Religion goes begging through the taverns. You charge admission to the temple floor, a fee for the sacred entrance; you can't know the gods for free — they're for sale.

What exactly do you do to honor them that you don't also do for your dead? Buildings, altars — same thing. The statues wear the same attire and insignia. Whatever the dead man's age, art, or trade was, that's what the god becomes. How does Jupiter's silicernium differ from a funeral feast, the obba from the simpulum, the pollinctor from the haruspex? Even the haruspex shows up for the dead.

So by all means, vote divine honors to dead emperors — you already attributed divinity to them while they were alive. Your gods will accept it; better yet, they'll congratulate themselves, since their masters have just been made their equals.

But when you worship Larentina, a public prostitute — or at least Lais or Phryne — among the Junos, Cereses, and Dianas; when you consecrate Simon Magus with a statue and an inscription as a holy god; when you promote some unknown palace tutor to a synod deity — the older gods may not be more noble, but they'll count it an insult from you that this privilege, which only antiquity conferred on them, has now been allowed to others.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the nuances of the Latin text, including the complex rhetorical structure and the specific list of deities and figures. Pass A provides a faithful literal translation, and Pass B provides a fluent rendering that preserves all semantic content, including the specific items (silicernium, obba, etc.) and the satirical tone regarding the commercialization of religion.
